I have a scar on my forearm from my own dog.
 
For four months I told everyone I got it from a bramble on a hike.
 
My coworkers. My mom. My best friend.
 
Nobody knew.
 
Because how do you tell someone that the dog you love — the dog you've had for three years, the dog who sleeps on your bed every night — turned around on a walk and bit you?
 
Not a stranger. Not a child. Not someone who provoked him.
 
Me.
 
The person who feeds him every morning. Who scratches his ears. Who spent $4,600 trying to fix his reactivity so he could have a better life.
 
It happened on a Tuesday afternoon in October.
 
We were on our usual route. Diesel spotted a dog about 40 feet ahead. He went into full reaction — lunging, barking, spinning.
 
I tried to redirect him the way the trainer taught me. Stepped in front of him. Said his name firmly.
 
He turned and bit my forearm.
 
One second. Clean puncture. Blood immediately.
 
I stood on that sidewalk holding my arm and I didn't cry. I just stared at him.
 
He was already calm again. Tail low. Looking at me like nothing had happened.
 
I walked home in silence.
 
Cleaned the wound in the bathroom with the door locked. Put a bandage on. Went and sat on the couch.
 
Diesel came and put his head in my lap.
 
And I sat there thinking: what is happening to us?
 
I'd had Diesel since he was 14 months old. Adopted him from a rescue. He was nervous at first — that's normal, they said. Give him time.
 
The reactivity started around month three.
 
Lunging at dogs on walks. Then at cyclists. Then at joggers.
 
I hired a trainer immediately. Positive reinforcement, counter-conditioning, all of it.
 
It helped. For about six weeks.
 
Then it stopped helping.
 
Second trainer. $140 per session. Eight sessions.
 
Better for a while. Then the same plateau.
 
By year two, Diesel was on Prozac.
 
It took the edge off. Some days.
 
Other days he was just as explosive as before the medication.
 
My vet said: "Some dogs need a higher dose. Some dogs just have a reactivity ceiling."
 
I didn't know what a reactivity ceiling was. But it didn't sound like something with a solution.
 
I kept going. Kept training. Kept medicating. Kept managing every single walk like a military operation.
 
Different side of the street. Treats ready. Eyes scanning ahead constantly.
 
And then October happened.
 
After he bit me, I didn't tell the trainer. I didn't tell the vet.
 
I was ashamed. And I was scared of what they might say.
 
That he was dangerous. That we'd reached the end of what was manageable.
 
I kept the bandage on for two weeks. Wore long sleeves until the scar faded enough that nobody would ask.
 
But I couldn't stop thinking about it.
 
He bit me.
 
And the worst part — the part I couldn't say out loud to anyone — was that I understood why.
 
He wasn't trying to hurt me. He was in a state of complete panic. His nervous system had completely overridden everything. He didn't see me in that moment.
 
He was just trying to escape something his brain told him was a threat.
 
And I had stepped into the middle of that.
 
But understanding it didn't make it less frightening.
 
Because if his brain could override his bond with me — what happened the next time a child ran up to him? What happened the next time someone reached out to pet him without asking?
 
I started researching obsessively. Not training techniques. Not medication dosages.
 
Why.
 
Why does a dog's brain override everything — even their attachment to the person they love

 once in three years.
 
Week 3: He saw a cyclist coming and didn't lunge. Slowed slightly. Kept moving.
 
Week 4: We walked past the spot where he bit me.
 
He didn't react to anything on that block.
 
I stood there for a moment after we passed it.
 
Week 6: I let him off leash in the backyard while my neighbor was in her yard next door with her dog.
 
He looked at the dog through the fence. Whined once. Walked away.
 
I sat down on the grass and just stayed there.
 
Eight weeks in, I told my best friend what really happened in October.
 
She was quiet for a long time.
 
"Why didn't you tell me?"
 
"I was ashamed."
 
"Of him or of yourself?"
 
I thought about it.
 
"Both."
 
Diesel has never bitten me again.
 
He's not a different dog. He still has moments. But his brain has a buffer now. His gut can produce what it was always supposed to produce.
 
The walks aren't military operations anymore.
 
And the thing I was most scared of — that his brain could completely override his bond with me — hasn't happened since.
 
If your dog has ever redirected onto you during a reactive episode — if you've been scratched, pulled down, or bitten and told someone a different story about where it came from — you're not alone.
 
And it's not because your dog doesn't love you.
 
It's because their gut can't produce what their brain needs to stay connected to you when panic hits.
 
Training can't fix that. Medication manages it but doesn't fix it. Only repairing the gut can fix it.
 
The only supplement I trust now: CalmAxis.

P.S. After Diesel bit me, I looked up what happens when a dog bites their owner and gets reported. In most states, a documented bite — even to a family member — can result in a dangerous dog classification. Once that classification exists, a second incident almost always means mandatory euthanasia. I never reported it. I was scared of what would happen to him. But I also knew I couldn't keep pretending the problem wasn't escalating. If your dog has redirected onto you — even once — please take it seriously. It's not a one-time thing. It's a warning from a broken system that's getting worse.
 
P.P.S. I'm not paid by CalmAxis. I'm just someone who wore long sleeves for four months because I was ashamed of a scar I didn't know how to explain. If this helps even one person avoid what I went through — or avoid losing their dog to something that had a biological cause all along — it's worth writing.

I was diagnosed with POTS at 29. I'm 34 now. Turns out my POTS was real, but nobody ever screened me for the thing that was actually causing my POTS to flare so badly, so often, that I couldn't work for five years.
For five years, I "managed" a condition without knowing what was firing it.

Five years of compression stockings pulled up to my thighs. I own eleven pairs. Class 2 medical grade. I put them on lying down every morning before I stood up. If I stood up without them my heart rate would jump from 68 to 148 within thirty seconds.
Five years of salt loading. Ten grams a day. Salt tabs, LMNT packets, broth in the morning, olives at lunch. My blood pressure ran on the low end of normal all the time. Without the salt, I'd faint.
Five years of a beta blocker my cardiologist prescribed to keep my heart rate from spiking when I stood up. It worked but it made me exhausted. Some days it made me too tired to shower.
Five years of ivabradine when the beta blocker stopped working alone. Then midodrine. Then fludrocortisone. My cardiologist called it "the standard POTS protocol." I called it "the reason I can't feel my hands after 3 p.m."
Five years of being handed a new modality — a tilt-table test that lasted forty-two minutes and had me in a puddle of tears by the end, a QSART sweat test, a full autonomic panel at a specialty clinic in Cleveland — and told to "just give it time."
I did everything they asked.

I did a "recumbent exercise protocol" designed for POTS patients. I could bike lying down for ten minutes at a time. That was my exercise. I did it three times a week for two years.
I saw a functional cardiologist who charged $2,400 for a consult and put me on a $520-a-month supplement stack that included NAD+ IV drips once a week. I stayed on it for eight months.
I did the Levine Protocol — a graded exercise program designed for POTS. I could not get past week 4. Every time I progressed, I would crash for the next week.
I saw a Mayo Clinic dysautonomia specialist. He confirmed the diagnosis. He said POTS is a lifelong management condition. He said the best I could hope for was a "functional baseline" that let me work part-time.
Part-time.
I was 29 when I was diagnosed. I had just made partner at my law firm. Three months later I could not stand up long enough to give a deposition.

I felt like I was crazy. The tilt-table was abnormal. My heart rate did what POTS heart rates do. But every single day, I could not understand why my nervous system had turned on me so completely, so suddenly.
By the time my alarm went off, I was already calculating. I lay in bed for twenty minutes doing my "pre-stand protocol" — drinking twenty ounces of water, doing leg lifts, taking my beta blocker, waiting for the salt tab to dissolve. Then I put on the compression stockings. Then I sat up slowly. Then I stood up.
Getting into the shower was a production. I sat on a shower chair. I kept the water lukewarm because hot water triggered a POTS flare. I washed my hair with my head tilted down because if I lifted my arms too long my heart rate would spike and I would faint.
By 10 a.m. I would be at my desk in compression stockings and a Camelbak of electrolyte water, working from home because I could not commute. I had left the law firm at year two. I was doing freelance contract work part-time. My income had dropped 70 percent.
By 2 p.m. I would hit what my POTS group called "the wall." Not the migraine wall — the POTS wall. My chest would feel tight. My h

ack to the law firm. Part-time first. Then full-time. My compression stockings are still in my drawer. I still take my beta blocker at a reduced dose. But I stand at my desk. I take stairs. I flew to New York for a client meeting last month and I sat upright the whole time.
I still have POTS. It didn't go away. But the cascade that was driving my POTS into disabling territory has quieted. And the difference between disabling POTS and manageable POTS is the difference between the me who couldn't work and the me who's back in a courtroom.

For almost three years, my nighttime routine looked like this.

10:45pm. Brush my teeth. Wash my face. Tell myself tonight is going to be different.

11:00pm. Get into bed. Tell my husband goodnight. He's already asleep. He sleeps like a normal person. I both love him and resent him for it.

11:04pm. Pick up my phone. Tell myself I'm just going to "check one thing."

11:47pm. Still on Instagram. Watching a stranger reorganize her pantry. 

Wondering if I should reorganize my pantry. Wondering why I care about her pantry.

12:23am. Now on TikTok. Watched a woman in Indiana make a charcuterie board for her teenager's birthday. I felt vaguely bad about my own life.

1:08am. Reading the comments under a Reddit post about a wedding I'm not invited to.

1:52am. Wondering why I'm still awake.

2:11am. Finally put the phone down. Eyes burning. Brain wired. 

Wake up at 6:45am feeling like I got hit by a truck.
If you're reading this, I'm willing to bet at least part of that schedule sounded familiar to you. 

Most of us are quietly doing some version of this and not really telling anyone, because it's embarrassing. It's the kind of habit you don't mention at brunch.

I'm 31. I work in HR. I'm married. I'm tired in a way that has become my baseline personality. 

My friends call it "tired in a sexy busy way," but really it's just tired.

I've known the phone was the problem for years. I didn't need a sleep specialist to tell me that. I just couldn't stop.
Here is the entire list of things I tried, in roughly the order I tried them.

I put my phone across the room at night. I'd just get out of bed and get it. I tried screen time limits. I'd hit "ignore for today" so fast my brain didn't register the prompt. I tried switching to a Kindle. 

I'd read for ten minutes and then sneak back to my phone for "just one thing." I tried a paperback. Same. 

I tried melatonin. I worked once, never again. 

I tried magnesium. I tried it for two months. Maybe it helped a little.
